how-to-depreciate-a-rental-property.html.text:

How to depreciate a rental property

Residential rental property is deducted over 27.5 years, the building only, with the first month counted as half. The arithmetic is short once you know which numbers go in. Here it is, with a worked example you can check against the tool.

The short version

  1. Start with the purchase price and add closing costs you must capitalize.
  2. Subtract the land. Land is never depreciated.
  3. Divide what is left by 27.5 for a full year of straight-line depreciation.
  4. In the first year, use the mid-month convention: count the month you started renting as half a month.
  5. Give every later improvement its own 27.5-year schedule from its own date.

A worked example

A rental bought for $250,000 with $5,000 of capitalized closing costs, of which $50,000 is land, and placed in service in June 2025:

StepAmount
Price + closing costs$255,000
Less land−$50,000
Depreciable basis (the building)$205,000
Full year: $205,000 ÷ 27.5$7,454.55
2025: 6.5 of 330 months (June counts as half)$4,037.88
2026 (a full year)$7,454.54
Each later full yearabout $7,454.55 (a cent either way as the running total rounds)

The yearly amounts add up to the basis exactly over the recovery period; the last year is a partial one. The figures above come from the same arithmetic Rental Ledger uses, so you can enter the same numbers and compare. They can differ from the IRS percentage tables by a few cents because the tables round to three decimals.

Where people lose money or get it wrong

  • Depreciating the land. It overstates the deduction and is easy for a preparer to spot.
  • Starting the clock at the purchase date. Depreciation starts when the property is ready and available to rent, which can be later.
  • Expensing an improvement. A new roof logged as a repair is deducted all at once when it should be spread over 27.5 years.
  • Forgetting what depreciation does at sale. It lowers your basis, so the gain on a sale is larger, and the part of it that is depreciation is taxed at up to 25%.
  • Missing the loss limits. A rental loss can be limited by the passive loss rules; the $25,000 allowance phases out between $100,000 and $150,000 of modified adjusted gross income.

Do it with your own numbers

Rental Ledger takes your properties, rent and expenses and produces Schedule E by property, the depreciation above, the passive loss allowance with carried-forward losses, and a sale-year estimate. It is free, needs no account and keeps everything on your device.

Common questions

How many years do you depreciate a residential rental property?

27.5 years, straight line, for residential rental property placed in service in the US. Only the building is depreciated; land is not, so the purchase price has to be split between the two.

What is the mid-month convention?

The property is treated as placed in service in the middle of the month, so the first calendar year gets a half month less than a full 12 months' worth. A home placed in service in June gets 6.5 months of depreciation in its first year, not 7.

What counts as the depreciable basis?

Generally the purchase price plus capitalized closing costs, minus the value of the land. The land share often comes from the county tax assessor's ratio of land to total value; if you have no better figure, ask your preparer.

Do improvements get their own depreciation clock?

Yes. A new roof or a kitchen remodel is depreciated over 27.5 years starting from the month it was placed in service, separately from the house. A repair that merely keeps the property in working order is deducted in the year paid. Telling the two apart is a judgment call, so Rental Ledger flags large repairs rather than deciding for you.

What if I never claimed depreciation?

Depreciation is treated as allowed whether or not you claimed it, which matters when you sell: the gain is computed as if you had taken it. If prior years were missed, a preparer can usually fix it with Form 3115 rather than amended returns.

Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?

No. Rental Ledger runs entirely in your browser; nothing you enter is uploaded.

Log rent and expenses against each property and get Schedule E by property, 27.5-year depreciation with the mid-month rule, the $25,000 passive loss allowance and what is suspended, a month-by-month rent collection grid and the contractors who need a 1099-NEC. No account, no bank link, and nothing leaves your device.

Tax year and your situation

1. Properties

One row per rental. Purchase price and land value set the depreciable basis; the date placed in service is when it was first ready to rent. Edit any cell and it saves.

Import a CSV

Columns: date,property,type,category,amount,vendor,note. Date is YYYY-MM-DD, property must match a name above, type is rent, deposit, expense, improvement or principal, category is an expense line such as repairs or insurance.

    3. Your numbers

      Schedule E, Part I, by property

      Rental loss rules (Form 8582, simple case)

      Rent collected by month

      Contractors to expect a 1099-NEC for

      Unincorporated payees you paid $2,000 or more for services in the year. Payments to corporations and for materials usually do not need one; confirm before filing.

        4. If you sell a property

        Estimates the federal tax on a sale: depreciation you took is recaptured at up to 25%, the rest is long-term gain, and the 3.8% investment income tax applies over $200,000 ($250,000 joint) of MAGI. Uses the properties and improvements above and the MAGI and suspended losses from the top. Nothing here is filed or sent anywhere.

          Back up, restore

          What it does and does not do

          • Fixed rules, no model. Depreciation, the passive loss allowance and the Schedule E columns are plain arithmetic you can check, to the cent.
          • Residential rentals. 27.5-year straight line, mid-month. Commercial property (39 years), short-term rentals with substantial services, cost segregation, bonus depreciation and sales are not modelled.
          • Federal only. No state rules, no qualified business income deduction, no net investment income tax, no real-estate-professional status, no at-risk limits.
          • Repairs versus improvements is your call. The page flags large repairs; you decide, with a preparer when the amount is large.
          • No bank sync, no tenant screening, no rent collection. That is the trade for being free and private. Import a CSV instead.

          Common questions

          Is this rental ledger really free?

          Yes. There is no account, no trial and no paywall. It runs in your browser, so it costs nothing to serve, and it stays free.

          Is anything uploaded?

          No. Your properties, rents and expenses are stored in your browser on this device and every sum is done there. There are no accounts, cookies or analytics vendors.

          Is this a replacement for Stessa, Baselane or a spreadsheet?

          It is a lighter, private alternative for a landlord with a handful of units who wants Schedule E by property without connecting a bank. There is no bank sync, no tenant portal and no rent collection. You enter or import rows, and it does the Schedule E, depreciation and passive-loss arithmetic.

          How is depreciation calculated?

          Residential rental property is depreciated straight line over 27.5 years with the mid-month convention: the month you place it in service counts as half. The basis is the price plus closing costs you add to basis, minus the land value, because land is never depreciated. Each improvement is depreciated separately from its own date.

          What is the $25,000 rental loss allowance?

          If you actively participate in managing your rental, you can deduct up to $25,000 of rental loss against other income. It shrinks by 50 cents for every dollar your modified adjusted gross income is over $100,000 and is gone at $150,000. Anything you cannot use is suspended and carried forward, which this page tracks.

          Is a security deposit income?

          Not when you receive it, if you will return it. Enter it as a deposit so it stays out of rent. It becomes income in the year you keep it for unpaid rent, and a deduction for damage you repair is a normal expense.

          Is a new roof a repair?

          Usually not. Work that betters, restores or adapts the property is an improvement that you depreciate, not a repair you deduct in one year. The page flags large repairs so you can decide, and items of $2,500 or less per invoice can often be expensed under the de minimis safe harbor if you elect it on your return.

          Can I import from a spreadsheet or my bank?

          Yes, from a CSV with the columns date, property, type, category, amount, vendor and note. Most banks let you export a CSV; add the property and type columns in a spreadsheet and import it. Rows that cannot be read are listed with the reason instead of being dropped silently.

Rental Ledger vs. a landlord spreadsheet

Most small landlords start with a spreadsheet, and for one property it works. The trouble starts with the mid-month first year, a clock for every improvement and a loss limit that carries over. This page compares the two on those jobs.

What each one is for

A spreadsheet is flexible and yours. For one property and one year it is often enough, and a preparer can open it anywhere. The cost is that every rule lives in a formula you wrote, and it only stays right as long as every row is copied correctly.

Rental Ledger keeps the same rows and applies the rules for you: depreciation, the loss allowance, the rent collection grid and the 1099 list. It shows the arithmetic and exports back to CSV.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Mid-month first-year depreciationBuilt in here; a formula you write and check in a sheet.
Separate clock per improvementBuilt in here; one block of cells per improvement in a sheet.
Passive loss allowance and carryforwardBuilt in here; a manual worksheet in a sheet.
Contractors owed a 1099-NECListed here at the $2,000 threshold; a pivot table in a sheet.
Short-term rentals, commercial property, state rulesA spreadsheet. Rental Ledger is federal and residential only.
Where the data livesYour browser storage here; a file you keep in a sheet. Neither is uploaded by us.

Common questions

Can a spreadsheet do rental depreciation and Schedule E?

Yes. A careful spreadsheet can. The hard parts are the mid-month first year, a separate clock for every improvement, and keeping the totals tied to the rows when you add a property or a year.

What does a spreadsheet not do for you?

It does not tell you that a large expense logged as a repair looks like an improvement, list the contractors who crossed the 1099-NEC threshold, carry a suspended passive loss forward, or estimate the tax on a sale. You have to build and maintain each of those yourself.

What does Rental Ledger not do that a spreadsheet can?

It is federal and residential only. A spreadsheet can be bent to cover short-term rentals, commercial 39-year property, state rules or anything else your preparer needs, because you control every cell.

Can I move between the two?

Yes. Rental Ledger imports a CSV of rows and exports Schedule E and all entries as CSV, so a preparer can open the result in any spreadsheet.

Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?

No. Rental Ledger runs entirely in your browser; nothing you enter is uploaded.

Verify every figure against the IRS instructions or with a tax preparer before you file. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss arising from their use.

Nothing leaves your browser. Rental Ledger runs entirely client-side and keeps your records in this browser's storage; nothing you enter is uploaded.

Nothing here says or implies that a spreadsheet is a bad way to keep rental records — it is a different job: a sheet you build and maintain yourself where Rental Ledger applies the rules for you.
